subject: Archaeology
title: The Last Day of Pompeii
description: A 60-second lesson on The Last Day of Pompeii.

hook.text: On August 24, 79 CE, Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii under 20 feet of volcanic ash in less than 24 hours.

buildup.text: Pliny the Younger watched from across the bay and wrote a detailed account — the first eyewitness report of an eruption.

discovery.text: Most victims died not from lava but from pyroclastic surges — superheated gas clouds traveling at 450 miles per hour.

twist.text: Many residents ignored early tremors and stayed home. Romans did not understand volcanoes as natural phenomena.

climax.text: About 2,000 of Pompeii's 11,000 residents died. Most had time to flee but chose not to leave their belongings.

punchline.text: They stayed for their possessions. The volcano took everything anyway.

quiz.question: What killed most victims at Pompeii?
options: Lava flows that engulfed the city streets
Pyroclastic surges — superheated gas clouds at 450 mph
Collapsing buildings from the weight of falling ash

details.summary: On August 24, 79 CE, Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii under six meters of volcanic ash and pumice. Pliny the Younger's eyewitness account and the archaeological record together reconstruct a terrifying sequence
details.whyItMatters: Pompeii's destruction preserved an entire Roman city in a single catastrophic moment. The combination of written testimony and physical evidence creates an unparalleled reconstruction of ancient disaster and daily life.
takeaways: Vesuvius erupted on August 24, 79 CE, burying Pompeii
Six meters of ash and pumice preserved the city intact
Pliny the Younger's account provides an eyewitness narrative

faq.question: How did most people in Pompeii die?
faq.answer: Most victims died from pyroclastic surges — superheated clouds of gas and rock traveling at hurricane speed. These surges reached temperatures of 300°C and killed instantly through thermal shock. Earlier phases killed people under collapsing roofs from accumulated pumice weight.

faq.question: Did anyone survive the eruption?
faq.answer: Yes. Most of Pompeii's roughly 20,000 residents fled during the early hours when pumice was still falling. An estimated 2,000 people who stayed or couldn't leave died in the subsequent pyroclastic surges. Survivors resettled in nearby towns and some returned to dig out valuables.
